The motivation is that most contact-map predictors rely on multiple-sequence-alignment (MSA) and evolutionary-profile information, which is unavailable for many proteins lacking homologous sequences, and generating such profiles is computationally intensive. The authors therefore seek a method that predicts contact maps without homologous information, addressing the limitation of the prior single-sequence method SSCpred, which performs adequately for proteins with few homologs but poorly for those with more effective homologs. The central hypothesis is that unsupervised deep-learning features from ESM-1b, concatenated with one-hot encoding and SPOT-1D-Single outputs, will outperform both the single-sequence baseline and MSA-based predictors for proteins with low effective number of homologs (Neff), and that an ensemble of models trained with different feature combinations will further improve performance. The method was evaluated on three independent test sets: SPOT-2018 (669 proteins), Neff1-2018 (46 proteins with Neff=1), and CASP14-FM (15 free-modeling targets). Results show a 15% improvement in F1-score over SSCpred on CASP14-FM, and improvements of 48.7% and 48.5% over TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact respectively on proteins without homologs (Neff=1) in the SPOT-2018 set. The method is also substantially faster than evolutionary-profile-based methods, making it suitable for large-scale prediction. The study uses a benchmark dataset from ProteinNet (50914 proteins before 2016, clustered at 95% sequence identity), reduced to 39120 proteins after homology filtering, then to 34691 training and 88 validation proteins after length filtering. The architecture uses a 12-block ResNet (the maximum depth trainable on the available GPU), with convolutional layers of channel size 64 and kernel size 3, trained with the Adam optimizer (learning rate 0.001), batch size 1, and early stopping of 3. Six models were trained with different feature combinations, predicting either inter-residue contacts as binary classification or inter-residue distances as distance bins. The ensemble (SPOT-Contact-Single) outperformed all individual models, with a 4% improvement over the second-best individual model on the validation set. On the Neff1-2018 example protein (5YKZ_A), SPOT-Contact-Single achieved an F1-score of 0.388, compared to 0.215 for SPOT-Contact, 0.235 for TrRosetta, and 0.252 for ESM-1b. The authors note that using ESM-1b attention maps limits direct contact-map prediction to proteins with fewer than 1024 amino acids, but argue this is acceptable since proteins are usually composed of domains with fewer than 1000 residues. In terms of computational efficiency, SPOT-Contact-Single made predictions in 116 seconds on CPU for the CASP14-FM dataset, 22 times faster than TrRosetta, and TrRosetta took 1926 seconds on GPU, 42 times slower than SPOT-Contact-Single. The authors acknowledge that profile-based predictors improve over SPOT-1D-Single as Neff increases, indicating that multiple-sequence alignment of homologous sequences can provide co-mutation information more effectively than unsupervised learning. The paper also notes that further improvement may come from using more advanced architectural models such as Transformer or Performer. The study contributes a fast, reasonably accurate alternative to evolution-based methods for large-scale protein contact-map prediction, particularly for proteins without homologs. The paper's findings are supported by quantitative results across multiple test sets and feature combinations, and the method's design is grounded in prior work on protein contact-map prediction and transformer language models.
